source_text: Superest, ne antiquitas suum quoque habuerit sacramentum, novitatem christianam recensere, quasi et de Deo aliam, ac proinde disciplina quoque aemulam, cujus sophia filios suos jugulare non norit. Plane alia in Christo et divinitas et voluntas et schola, martyria aut nulla in totum, aut aliter intelligenda mandarit, qui neminem ad hujusmodi discrimen hortetur, qui pro eo passis nihil repromittat, quia pati eos nolit. Et ideo praeceptorum principia deducens: Beati, inquit, qui persecutionem patiuntur ob justitiam, quoniam illorum est regnum coelorum. Hoc quidem absolute ad omnes, dehinc proprie ad Apostolos ipsos: Beati eritis cum vos dedecoraverint, et persecuti fuerint, et dixerint adversus vos omnia mala propter me; gaudete et exultate, quoniam merces vestra plurima in coelo: sic enim faciebant et prophetis patres eorum. Ut etiam prophetaret quod et ipsi occidi haberent ad exemplum prophetarum. Quanquam et si omnem hanc persecutionem conditionalem in solos tunc Apostolos destinasset, utique per illos cum toto sacramento, cum propagine nominis, cum traduce Spiritus Sancti in nos quoque spectasset etiam persecutionis obeundae disciplina, ut in haereditarios discipulos, et apostolici seminis frutices. Nam et rursus ad Apostolos dirigit: Ecce ego mitto vos tanquam oves in medio luporum; et: Cavete ab hominibus; tradent enim vos in consessus, et in synagogis suis flagellabunt vos, et ad praesides et reges perducemini, mei caussa, in testimonium illis et nationibus, etc. Cum autem subjicit: Tradet autem frater fratrem, et pater filium in mortem, et insurgent filii in parentes, et mortificabunt eos; manifeste iniquitatem istam in caeteros pronuntiavit, quam in Apostolis non invenimus. Nemo enim eorum aut fratrem aut patrem passus est traditorem, quod plerique jam nostri.
pass_a_gloss: It remains, that the antiquity may also have had its own sacrament, to review the Christian novelty, as if there is also another God, and therefore a rival discipline, whose wisdom does not know how to slaughter its own sons. Clearly, in Christ there is another divinity and will and school, either no martyrdoms at all, or they are to be understood in a different way, by the one who exhorts no one to this kind of danger, who promises nothing to those who suffer for Him, because He does not want them to suffer. And therefore, drawing out the principles of the teachings: Blessed, He says, are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, because the kingdom of heaven is theirs. This indeed is said absolutely to all, then properly to the Apostles themselves: Blessed will you be when they insult you, and persecute you, and say all evil things against you on account of me; rejoice and exult, because your reward is very great in heaven: for thus they did to the prophets, their fathers. So that He might also prophesy that they themselves would be killed, as an example of the prophets. Although even if He had destined this entire conditional persecution only to the Apostles at that time, certainly through them, with the whole sacrament, with the propagation of the name, with the transmission of the Holy Spirit to us, He would also have looked to the discipline of undergoing persecution, as to the heirs of the disciples, and the fruits of the apostolic seed. For again He addresses the Apostles: Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves; and: Beware of men; for they will hand you over to councils, and they will flog you in their synagogues, and you will be led before governors and kings, for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations, etc. When, however, He adds: A brother will hand over a brother to death, and a father a son, and sons will rise up against parents, and will kill them; He clearly pronounces this wickedness against others, which we do not find in the Apostles. For none of them suffered a brother or a father as a betrayer, which many of ours have already done.

pass_b_english: If the old order has its own sacrament, we must examine the Christian innovation—unless we are prepared to admit another God, and thus a rival discipline, whose wisdom does not know how to slaughter its own sons. In Christ, the divinity, the will, and the school are clearly different: either there are no martyrdoms at all, or they must be understood differently by the One who urges no one into such danger, who promises nothing to those who suffer for Him, because He does not want them to suffer. And so, laying out the principles of His teaching: "Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matt. 5:10–12). That promise is absolute, addressed to everyone; then He narrows it to the Apostles themselves: "Blessed are you when they revile you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you on my account; rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets before you" (Matt. 5:11–12). He was thereby prophesying that they, too, would be killed, following the pattern of the prophets. Even if He had destined this conditional persecution solely for the Apostles at that moment, He would still have had in view—through them, with the whole sacrament, the propagation of the Name, and the transmission of the Holy Spirit to us—the discipline of enduring persecution for the heirs of the disciples, the fruits of the apostolic seed. For He speaks again to the Apostles: "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves" (Matt. 10:16), and "Beware of men; for they will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues, and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations" (Matt. 10:17–18). But when He adds, "Brother will deliver brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death" (Matt. 10:21), He plainly pronounces this wickedness upon others—a treachery we do not find among the Apostles. None of them suffered a brother or a father as a betrayer, yet many of our own have already done so.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal gloss, while Pass B provides a fluent translation with necessary scripture citations (Matthew 5:10–12, 5:11–12, 10:16, 10:17–18, 10:21) which are correctly identified based on the quoted content. The distinction between the Apostles and 'our own' (the contemporary betrayers) is preserved.
